video.title: $1K a Day From This Simple Side Hustle (Here’s How to Copy It)

summary: Chris Koerner visits Clayton and Haley Bowman, a couple in Cameron, Missouri who run a family pizza tent in a hardware store parking lot, selling pizzas for $15-20. They say 20 orders is $600-700 in a day, with about 20% food cost and 15% other costs for roughly 60% profit, and some nights exceed $1,000; they pay for the spot with occasional lunches. Their advice is to start local and buy used equipment rather than waiting for everything new. Chris then cites other pizza operators (a UK trailer, a California professor at farmers markets claiming $175k net) and demonstrates his home dough recipe and Gozney-style oven technique. Key takeaway: a low-cost pop-up pizza business can have high margins but is entirely physical labour.

tactics.name: Free pitch in exchange for goodwill
steps: Approach a high-traffic local business (hardware store) with a parking lot
Offer free lunch occasionally instead of rent
Pitch the mutual benefit: pizza customers may shop at the store

tactics.name: Start cheap and upgrade later
steps: Start local, then expand across the state
Buy used equipment to launch faster
Replace equipment as the business grows
Move from tent to food truck, later a bakery/commissary producing dough for several trucks

quote.text: If we would have gotten you know just used stuff and we probably would have gotten out a little quicker
quote.speaker: Clayton Bowman

tactics.name: Neapolitan-style home dough recipe
steps: 65% hydration dough: 1 kg flour, water (stated as 65 g, meaning about 650 g), 25 g salt, 2 g yeast, splash of olive oil
Rest an hour on the counter, then 2 days covered in the fridge
Split into eight 200 g balls, proof about 2 hours
Dust with 50/50 00 flour and cornmeal; stretch with fists without pinching the edges; never use a rolling pin
Bake above 800F (turn down near 925F) for 60-90 seconds, rotating

quote.text: let it sit on the counter for an hour, cover it, put it in the fridge for 2 days
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Barter for a pitch: high-traffic host businesses may give free space in exchange for goodwill and extra foot traffic.
Food-service margins can be high (20% food cost) when you control labour yourself, but the work is fully physical.

lessons.lesson: Launch with used gear and upgrade gradually instead of waiting for a perfect setup.

lessons.lesson: Start local and expand outward once the product is proven.

lessons.lesson: A central bakery/commissary that supplies dough can enable multiple food trucks later.
Skill can be self-taught through repetition; expect early versions to be bad.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand numbers from a very small operator plus second-hand examples; Chris's 80-90% margin claim is promotional framing.
